title: Socket Server Lifecycle
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Robotics and Computational Thinking
description: A p5.js step-through of the Chapter 11 robot web server. A two-column lifecycle shows the browser (client) and the Pico W server calls socket, bind, listen, accept, recv, handle_cmd, send, and close, with a blocking indicator on accept(), a listen(1) queue for one waiting browser, refused connections, and motors that run after a POST cmd=forward.

educational.topic: Socket programming for a microcontroller web server
learningObjectives: Order the socket calls a web server makes: socket, bind, listen, accept, recv, send, close
Explain that accept() blocks until a browser connects and returns a new socket for that browser
Explain why listen(1) lets only one browser wait and refuses extra connections
Explain why s.close() belongs in a finally block
prerequisites: HTTP GET and POST and socket programming from Chapter 11
while loops and try/finally from Chapter 4

controls.label: Auto Play
controls.purpose: Step automatically, pausing while accept() is blocked

controls.label: Reset
controls.purpose: Restart the server program (a second Reset after an error unplugs and replugs the robot)

controls.label: Browser A connects
controls.purpose: A browser opens a connection to port 80

controls.label: Browser B connects
controls.purpose: A second browser connects, possibly while the server is busy

simulation.modelType: Step-through state machine of a single-threaded socket server
assumptions: listen(1) holds one waiting connection; extra connections are refused
The server handles one browser completely before calling accept() again
Without s.close(), restarting the program leaves port 80 in use until the board is reset
limitations: Does not model TCP handshakes, timeouts, or partial reads
Real network stacks may queue slightly more connections than the listen() number

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Worked example with step-through and what-if events
pedagogical.interactionPattern: Next Step / Auto Play lifecycle diagram with browser event buttons
keyQuestions: Which call makes the robot stop and wait?
What does accept() give back, and how is conn different from s?
What happens to a third browser while the robot is busy?
Why does forgetting s.close() cause an error on the next run?
commonMisconceptions: The server socket s is used to talk to the browser (a new socket conn is used)
The robot can serve many browsers at the same time
The robot keeps working on other tasks while it waits in accept()
assessmentOpportunities: Ordering the nine steps before and after the sim
Explaining the fate of each browser in the queue experiment
Exit ticket about three simultaneous browsers
